notes.meaning: Issachar's tribe was divided into four main clans named after his four sons. These match the sons who went down into Egypt years earlier, though one son named Job in Genesis is called Jashub here. Both forms of that name come from the same root meaning to return.
The fighting men of Issachar numbered 64,300. That was an increase of 9,900 men since the first census at Mount Sinai. God blessed this tribe with steady growth during their years in the wilderness.

Zebulun was divided into three clans founded by his sons Sered, Elon, and Jahleel. These names are the same as those listed when the family first settled in Egypt. All three family lines remained intact throughout the wilderness journey.
Zebulun counted 60,500 men ready for service. That was an increase of 3,100 men from the first count. Like the other tribes encamped under Judah's standard, Zebulun grew rather than shrank.

Joseph's household was counted as two full tribes through his sons Manasseh and Ephraim. Jacob had adopted both grandsons as his own sons before he died, giving Joseph a double share. Because of that adoption, both brothers founded separate tribal territories.

Manasseh's family line ran through his son Machir down to his grandson Gilead. Both of these men founded large, respected clans within the tribe. Gilead's descendants went on to form several prominent branches of their own.

Six clans came from the sons of Gilead: Iezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Shemida, and Hepher. Along with Machir and Gilead, they gave Manasseh eight leading family groups. Each of these clans would receive a designated share of land in Canaan.

Zelophehad had five daughters and no sons to carry on his name. He is highlighted here because having only daughters was unusual among the clan leaders. This special mention prepares the way for God's ruling about daughters inheriting family land.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that while the daughters won the right to inherit property, the later rule requiring them to marry inside their tribe kept the land under male tribal control.

notes.meaning: Manasseh's registered men totaled 52,700. This was a jump of 20,500 men from the first census, making it the fastest-growing tribe in Israel. This great increase fulfilled the ancient blessing spoken over Joseph's descendants.

Ephraim's tribe was arranged into clans through his sons Shuthelah, Becher, and Tahan, along with his grandson Eran. These four groups formed the backbone of the tribe. They preserved their family records carefully as they prepared to cross into the promised land.

Ephraim numbered 32,500 fighting men, which was 8,000 fewer than at Mount Sinai. Even though Jacob had promised Ephraim greater prominence than Manasseh, Ephraim was currently the smaller of the two. God's promises are completely dependable, but they often take time to appear.

Benjamin was counted through five clans named after his sons. Benjamin originally had ten sons when Israel entered Egypt, but five of those lines seem to have died out childless. God still kept the surviving families strong and preserved their place in the nation.

Two of Bela's sons, Ard and Naaman, became heads of their own distinct clans. These two grandson lines brought Benjamin's total recognized clans to seven. Through them, God built up the tribe even after earlier family lines were lost.
Benjamin counted 45,600 men of fighting age. That was an increase of 10,200 men over their first census number. Even with fewer original sons, the tribe flourished under God's care.

Dan had only one main clan listed, named after his son Shuham. In Genesis this son was called Hushim, which is another form of the very same name. From this single family branch, an entire tribe grew.

The single clan of Shuham numbered 64,400 fighting men. This made Dan the second largest tribe in all of Israel, behind only Judah. It proved that human advantages do not determine growth, since increase comes entirely from God's blessing.
